en: I am standing in the queue at the bank.
context: Telling a friend where you are on the phone.
explain: Present continuous with 'am' shows an action happening right now.
usage: Use it on a phone call when someone asks where you are.
leelaQ: Do you like going to the bank, or do you prefer online banking?
answer: I prefer online banking because it saves a lot of time.

en: Can I open a savings account here today?
tamil: நான் இன்னைக்கு இங்க சேமிப்பு கணக்கு தொடங்கலாமா?
context: Asking a bank clerk about a new account.
explain: 'Can I ...?' is a simple way to ask for permission or possibility.
usage: Say this to the bank staff at the help desk when you want a new account.
leelaQ: Do you have a savings account? Which bank is it in?
answer: Yes, I have a savings account in a government bank.

en: I paid the electricity bill online yesterday.
context: Telling your father the bill is already paid.
explain: 'Paid' is the past form of 'pay'. 'Yesterday' tells us when it happened.
usage: Use it at home when family asks whether a bill is paid.
leelaQ: How do you pay your electricity bill every month?
answer: I pay it online using my phone.

en: Could you please check my balance?
tamil: என் இருப்பை கொஞ்சம் பார்த்து சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Asking a bank employee for help.
explain: 'Could you please ...?' is a very polite way to request something.
usage: Use it politely with a bank clerk or at an ATM kiosk helper.
leelaQ: How often do you check your bank balance?
answer: I check my balance once a week.

en: I do not have change for five hundred rupees.
context: Telling an auto driver you have no small notes.
explain: 'Change' here means small notes and coins. 'Do not have' shows you lack something.
usage: Say it to a driver or shopkeeper when you only have a big note.
leelaQ: What do you do when a shop has no change for you?
answer: I pay by UPI instead of using cash.

en: I will transfer the money to your account tonight.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு ராத்திரி உங்க கணக்குக்கு பணம் அனுப்பறேன்.
context: Promising a friend to send money.
explain: 'Will' shows a promise or decision made for the future.
usage: Use it with a friend or relative who is waiting for money.
leelaQ: Have you ever sent money to a friend? How did you do it?
answer: Yes, I sent money to my friend using a mobile app.

en: Which UPI app do you use for payments?
tamil: நீங்க பணம் கட்ட எந்த UPI ஆப் பயன்படுத்தறீங்க?
context: Chatting with a colleague about phone payments.
explain: 'Which' is used when we choose from a few known options.
usage: Ask it casually with friends or colleagues when talking about apps.
leelaQ: What do you usually pay for using your phone?
answer: I pay for groceries and auto fares using my phone.

en: I have saved ten thousand rupees this year.
context: Proudly telling a friend about your savings.
explain: Present perfect 'have saved' links a past action to the present result.
usage: Use it when you talk about your savings goals with friends or family.
leelaQ: How much do you want to save this year?
answer: I want to save twenty thousand rupees this year.

en: Please scan this QR code to pay.
tamil: பணம் கட்ட இந்த QR கோடை ஸ்கேன் பண்ணுங்க.
context: A shopkeeper asking a customer to pay by phone.
explain: 'Please' makes an order sound polite. 'To pay' tells the purpose.
usage: A shop owner says this at the counter when a customer wants to pay by UPI.
leelaQ: Do you pay by QR code in small shops?
answer: Yes, most small shops near my house accept QR codes.

en: You should keep your ATM PIN secret.
context: Advising an elderly relative about card safety.
explain: 'Should' gives advice. 'Keep ... secret' means do not tell anyone.
usage: Use it when you advise family members about safe banking.
leelaQ: How do you keep your bank details safe?
answer: I never tell my PIN to anyone.

en: Did the payment go through on your phone?
context: Asking a friend after a UPI payment.
explain: 'Go through' means a payment or request was successful.
usage: Ask it right after someone pays in a shop or on a call.
leelaQ: Has a payment ever failed for you? What did you do?
answer: Yes, once it failed, so I tried again after some time.

en: My salary comes into my account on the first of every month.
tamil: என் சம்பளம் மாசம் ஒண்ணாம் தேதி என் கணக்குல வரும்.
context: Telling a friend when you get paid.
explain: Simple present is used for regular habits and fixed schedules.
usage: Use it when you talk about your monthly money plan.
leelaQ: When do you get your salary or pocket money?
answer: I get my pocket money on the first of every month.

en: The card payment did not work at the shop.
context: Explaining a payment problem to a friend.
explain: 'Did not work' is the negative past. The verb 'work' stays in base form.
usage: Use it to explain why you had to pay in cash or try another way.
leelaQ: What do you do if your card does not work?
answer: I pay with cash or use my phone.

en: I am making a budget for the next month.
context: Telling your spouse about monthly planning.
explain: Present continuous shows work in progress. 'Make a budget' is a common phrase.
usage: Use it at home when you plan monthly spending with your family.
leelaQ: What are the main things in your monthly budget?
answer: Rent, food and travel are the main things in my budget.

en: When will the loan be approved?
context: Asking a bank officer about your loan.
explain: 'Will be approved' is a passive future form. It focuses on the loan, not the person.
usage: Ask it at the bank when you are waiting for a loan decision.
leelaQ: What would you take a loan for, if you needed one?
answer: I would take a loan to buy a house.

en: Can you give me a receipt for this payment?
tamil: இந்த பணத்துக்கு ஒரு ரசீது தர முடியுமா?
context: Asking a shopkeeper for proof of payment.
explain: 'Can you give me ...?' is a simple polite request.
usage: Say it at a shop, school office or clinic after you pay.
leelaQ: Why is it good to keep a receipt?
answer: It is good because I can show it if there is a problem.

en: I forgot my debit card at home today.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு என் டெபிட் கார்டை வீட்டுலயே மறந்துட்டேன்.
context: Telling a friend why you cannot pay by card.
explain: 'Forgot' is the past of 'forget'. 'At home' tells where the card is.
usage: Use it with friends or colleagues when you cannot pay.
leelaQ: What do you do when you forget your wallet at home?
answer: I use my phone to pay.

en: I am going to pay the loan instalment on Friday.
context: Telling someone your plan for a loan payment.
explain: 'Am going to' talks about a plan you have already made.
usage: Use it with a bank officer or family when you speak of a payment plan.
leelaQ: What payments do you have to make every month?
answer: I have to pay rent and a phone bill every month.

en: How much is the interest on this loan?
context: Asking a loan officer about the cost.
explain: 'How much' asks for an amount. Interest is the extra money you pay on a loan.
usage: Ask it before you take a loan from a bank or a finance office.
leelaQ: Why should we ask about interest before taking a loan?
answer: Because interest decides how much extra money we must pay.

en: The bank closes at four in the afternoon.
context: Warning a friend about bank timing.
explain: Simple present is used for fixed timings.
usage: Use it to tell someone to hurry before the bank shuts.
leelaQ: What time do shops near your house close?
answer: They close at nine at night.

en: You must not share your OTP with anyone.
context: Warning a parent about fraud calls.
explain: 'Must not' is a strong rule. It shows something is forbidden or dangerous.
usage: Say it to family or friends to protect them from phone fraud.
leelaQ: What should we do if a stranger asks for our OTP?
answer: We should cut the call and tell the bank.

en: Please fill this form and sign here.
tamil: இந்த படிவத்தை நிரப்பி இங்க கையெழுத்து போடுங்க.
context: A bank clerk giving instructions to a customer.
explain: Two actions joined by 'and'. 'Please' keeps the tone polite.
usage: Bank and office staff use this when a customer must complete a form.
leelaQ: Do you find forms easy or difficult to fill?
answer: I find them a little difficult because they are long.

en: The money has reached my account.
context: Telling a friend the payment arrived.
explain: 'Has reached' shows the money came and is there now.
usage: Use it after a friend or customer says they sent money.
leelaQ: How do you know when money comes into your account?
answer: I get an SMS from the bank.

en: Should I take a loan for a new bike?
context: Asking a friend for advice on buying a bike.
explain: 'Should I ...?' asks for advice or an opinion.
usage: Ask it with an elder, a friend or a bank agent before a big purchase.
leelaQ: Would you buy a bike with a loan or with savings?
answer: I would buy it with savings because loans cost more.

en: We spent too much on groceries last month.
tamil: போன மாசம் மளிகைக்கு ரொம்ப செலவு பண்ணிட்டோம்.
context: Talking with your wife about household expenses.
explain: 'Too much' means more than needed. 'Spent' is the past of 'spend'.
usage: Use it when you review the family budget at home.
leelaQ: How can a family spend less on groceries?
answer: We can make a list and buy only what we need.
